candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Physical instantiation explains only part of mathematical applicability, because indispensable structures such as Hilbert spaces and complex numbers cannot themselves be physically instantiated, whereas theism can explain their predictive usefulness.
candidates.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly shifts from Oppy's question to Craig's qualified answer, followed by his characteristic appeal to Steiner and the comparative explanatory power of theism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move supplies Craig's central reason for denying that structural instantiation alone resolves the debate and directly advances the claim that theism explains a broader range of mathematical applicability.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Oppy's proposed account on which mathematical theories apply because the physical world instantiates the structures they describe.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy first reconstructs Craig's proposal as divine selection of a mathematically structured world. Craig accepts that reconstruction only in part and argues that non-instantiable mathematical structures still require explanation.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Craig's appeal to approximate correspondence is unclear because superseded theories can misdescribe or add physical structure, making it difficult to say how they genuinely latch onto the world's structure.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly frames the passage as an attempt to understand Craig's account, uses sustained first-person questioning, and develops examples involving Neptune, Newtonian mechanics, and general relativity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move challenges the coherence of the proposed relation between mathematical theories and physical structure, thereby pressing a central explanatory component of Craig's theistic account.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that even imperfect mathematical theories latch onto physical structure to useful degrees of approximation.

candidates.contextSummary: After Craig says non-instantiable mathematics can still describe and predict phenomena, Oppy probes what relation connects such theories to the world and argues that approximation is difficult to characterize.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Whether a theory adds or removes structure, its physical adequacy is measured by descriptive accuracy and predictive success, and the unexpected mathematical success exhibited by improved theories favors theism over naturalism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig answers the immediately preceding challenge, refers to his own views about general relativity and simultaneity, and concludes with an explicit comparison of theism and naturalism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This response defends the applicability claim against Oppy's approximation objection and reconnects the technical discussion directly to the debate's comparative explanatory conclusion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Oppy's objection that added or erroneous structure makes the notion of one physical theory approximating another difficult to understand.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy argues that Newtonian mechanics may contain extra structure rather than merely approximate general relativity. Craig answers that empirical accuracy and successful prediction determine adequacy despite structural additions or deletions.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: The many mathematically generated solutions and predictions that fail to correspond to physical reality may undermine claims of uncanny effectiveness, since attention may be selectively focused on rare successes such as the positron.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy announces that he will address the effectiveness question, develops a detailed projectile-model example, and contrasts Dirac's successful positron prediction with magnetic monopoles and other failures.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly disputes the evidential datum that mathematical applicability is unusually successful or surprising, attacking the first-stage premise needed for the proposed inference to theism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's contention that mathematical descriptions and predictions display an unexpected accuracy that theism explains better than naturalism.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig has defended mathematical applicability by emphasizing descriptive and predictive success. Oppy replies that models routinely yield discarded solutions and theories yield failed predictions, creating a possible selection effect.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: The predominance of failed mathematical applications is expected given infinite mathematics and a finite physical world, but those failures do not explain the breathtaking precision of the successful applications under naturalism.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker cites Wigner and Steiner, concedes that failures outnumber successes, and then explicitly argues that this concession does not make successful precision likely on naturalism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's direct defense of the surprising-applicability datum against Oppy's selection-effect objection and preserves the principal premise supporting the comparative theistic inference.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Oppy's suggestion that failed mathematical predictions and discarded model solutions may remove any genuinely uncanny pattern of effectiveness.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy argues that remembered successes may be exceptional among numerous mathematical failures. Craig accepts the numerical predominance of failures but denies that it reduces the explanatory significance of extraordinarily precise successes.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: A naturalistic modal theory can explain mathematical applicability by treating the laws and boundary conditions as necessary and necessarily amenable to mathematical formulation, with contingency confined to how chances unfold.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly turns from questioning the datum to presenting his own naturalistic explanation, identifies its modal commitments, and states how necessity explains the observed effectiveness of mathematics.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move presents the principal naturalistic rival explanation and directly denies the debate's central claim that naturalism lacks resources comparable to theism for explaining applicability.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's repeated assertion that naturalism cannot explain why successful mathematical descriptions exhibit such striking precision and applicability.

candidates.contextSummary: After discussion of whether applicability is genuinely uncanny, Oppy grants the relevant fit for argument's sake and outlines a naturalistic metaphysics in which mathematical formulability follows necessarily from the laws and boundary conditions.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Oppy's necessity postulate is implausible because no physical universe, or a chaotic universe inaccessible to mathematical understanding, appears metaphysically possible, making the world's mathematical order contingent rather than necessary.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig directly addresses Oppy by name, targets the necessity claim, offers counterpossibilities, and supports the contingency of mathematical order with an extended attribution to Einstein.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move attacks the foundational modal premise of Oppy's naturalistic explanation and restores the contingency and surprisingness required for Craig's comparative argument for theism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Oppy's naturalistic modal theory that the laws, boundary conditions, and their amenability to mathematical formulation hold necessarily.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy has proposed that necessity itself explains mathematical applicability. Craig responds that physical reality could have been absent or chaotic and invokes Einstein to reinforce the claim that objective mathematical order was not antecedently expected.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: The modal proposal is offered as the best overall metaphysical theory rather than an a priori expectation, because it balances limited theoretical commitments with broad explanation and shows that naturalism does possess an explanation.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy distinguishes metaphysical from epistemic expectation, explicitly calls the view his best metaphysical theory, and explains its comparative virtues in terms of commitment and explanatory scope.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This response clarifies the epistemic status of Oppy's naturalistic account and shifts the dispute from whether naturalism has an explanation to which complete metaphysical theory is better overall.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's objection that alternative universes and Einstein's expectation of chaos show mathematical order to be contingent rather than necessary.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that mathematical order could have failed and therefore cannot be necessary. Oppy replies that his claim concerns the best total metaphysical theory, whose merits must be assessed against all relevant data.

candidates.speaker: Graham Oppy
candidates.proposition: Divine freedom creates a dilemma: if God could not create a world without mathematical applicability, the theist accepts the naturalist's necessity explanation; if God could, the actual applicability rests on an unexplained brute divine choice.
candidates.attributionBasis: Oppy asks Craig a direct question about divine freedom and then explicitly lays out two exhaustive options, deriving necessity on one branch and brute contingency on the other.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The dilemma directly challenges the claim that theism provides greater explanatory depth, arguing that its appeal to divine choice either collapses into necessity or terminates in brute contingency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's proposal that God freely fashions a physical world whose structure and behavior make mathematical theories strikingly applicable.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of mathematical order and fine-tuning, Oppy asks whether God could have chosen a non-mathematically applicable world and argues that either possible answer undermines the claimed explanatory advantage of theism.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Ultimately inexplicable free divine choices are unproblematic, and a theistic account containing such choices still has greater explanatory depth than merely postulating the necessity of the world's mathematical structure.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator requests a quick response, after which Craig accepts ultimate inexplicability in divine choice and explicitly contrasts the explanatory depth of that view with necessity.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This concise response directly answers Oppy's central dilemma and states why Craig believes brute divine choice does not eliminate theism's comparative explanatory advantage.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Oppy's dilemma that divine freedom makes mathematical applicability either necessary, as naturalism claims, or an unexplained brute contingency.

candidates.contextSummary: Oppy argues that theism must choose between necessity and brute contingency. Craig accepts that free choices can be ultimately inexplicable while maintaining that the broader theistic account remains explanatorily deeper.
